subject: plagueDoctor
pitch:
Category: Humanoid character.
Subject: plague doctor with lantern.
Style: Darkest Dungeon.
reasoning:
I'm planning a Darkest Dungeon-style plague doctor as a full TypeScript module of roughly 700-1100 lines, with a rigged humanoid in an A-pose—arms angled down rather than a strict T-pose—so the lantern can hang naturally from one hand.

The aesthetic calls for a dark, gothic palette with heavy ink outlines, desaturated tones, crimson accents, and rusty metals, plus a beaked leather mask, wide-brimmed hat, cloak, satchel of vials, and a warm glowing lantern. I'm now sketching out the skeleton hierarchy—hips, spine chain to chest, neck, and head—with specific joint coordinates for a roughly 1.8m figure, including a separate upper and lower jaw for the mask's mouth.

I'm planning the head joint and splitting the beak into upper and lower jaw pieces so it can open, then working through arm placement in an A-pose with shoulder-elbow-hand chains using local axis conventions for simplicity.

Computing joint positions...

Now naming the arm chain: shoulder, elbow, wrist with three names so the wrist becomes a tip joint aimed along the final segment's direction. I'll move on to setting up the finger joints next.

For hands I'll give each four finger chains plus a thumb, each finger being a short two-joint chain, keeping the total joint count well within budget. The lantern will hang from the left hand via its own joint parented to the wrist, dangling from a strap or hook so it visually reads as being held while fingers stay naturally extended.

The right hand I'll leave empty since the plague doctor's signature items are the lantern and belt vials/satchel rather than a staff or cane. Now I'm laying out the leg joint positions—hips, knees, and ankles—scaled proportionally down the leg.

For the lower body, I'm thinking heavy boots with a cuff, mostly covered by a long greatcoat flaring down to about 0.35m. The tricky part is rigging the coat skirt so it moves naturally with the legs underneath, likely as a rigid lathe shape attached to the hip bone, possibly with a front opening gap.

Rather than true split panels, I'll just lathe a simple cone-shaped skirt from waist to hem and fake the front slit with painted seam lines and buttons -- good enough visually, with legs and boots emerging from underneath.

Actually, for more character I'll build the skirt as several overlapping tattered blade panels, plus a short cape capelet lathed as a cone, with jagged hanging hem cards for that Darkest Dungeon tattered-cloak look. For the torso, I'll loft the coat body along the spine from hips to neck, then add a belt with buckle and a bandolier strap across the chest holding glowing green vials -- though glow effects need flat-colored parts rather than painted textures. Then I'll move to the head, building a skull shape hidden beneath the hood and hat.

For the plague doctor mask, I'll go with bone-ivory leather with stitching, brass-rimmed round lenses glowing faint amber-green, a black wide-brimmed hat with a crimson band, buckle, and a crow feather, plus a dark cowl draping from the hood down to the shoulders. Now I'm sweeping a curved cone shape forward and downward off the head to form the mask's beak.

Still building beak geometry...

Now I'm adding the hat: a lathed brim and crown sitting on the head bone, with a crimson band and brass buckle, making sure the brim clears the eyes from the front. For the hood I'm considering a partial sphere geometry with phi/theta angles so it forms an open cowl around the head instead of fully enclosing the face.

I'm working out the layering: a scaled sphere positioned slightly behind the head forms the hood, while a separate smaller sphere pushed forward forms the mask/face, adjusting radii and z-offsets so the hood frames the face without swallowing it.

Then I'm planning a torus around the mask opening for a cowl rim, a lathed capelet shell draping from neck to shoulders (accepting that the arms will poke through its surface, which could be softened with tattered edge cards), and finally a lofted coat body running along the spine with widening stations from hips to chest, bound to a hip/spine bone chain.

For the limbs, I'm sweeping tapered tube geometry along the arm chain for sleeves with a flared cuff at the wrist, then adding a turned-back leather cuff and gloves built from a palm box plus swept finger digits. I'm working out the hand's local orientation so the box geometry aligns correctly with the wrist joint's frame, using the arm's forward/down-out direction and keeping the roll toward the model's right.

I'm now computing the exact local axes at the wrist for the left arm: projecting a near-world-X vector perpendicular to the arm direction to get local X (down-right), then taking the cross product with local Y to confirm local Z points forward. This tells me the hand box's width runs across the arm plane along X while its thickness runs forward along Z, which determines how the palm faces.

For the T-pose with palms down, I realize the flat hand plane should actually contain the arm direction and the forward Z axis rather than X, so I'll set the hand box thickness along X, length along Y, and width along Z, with fingers fanning forward-back and the thumb pointing forward.

Placing finger joints by offsetting along the local Z axis at the knuckle, then building each finger as a two-joint chain extending from wrist position using the frame's own local axes.

So local axes map to [palm-normal, along-arm, forward] for both arms. Checking the palm-normal direction for each side: left gives a down-inward normal, right gives an up-outward one, which seems inconsistent given the mirrored geometry — I need to double check the handedness.

To avoid this confusion entirely, I'll switch to using the model's word-based directions (forward, down, etc.) for wrist orientation rather than raw local vectors, and compute along-arm offsets separately using the arm direction vector.

For the fingers, I'm setting up chains built from knuckle, mid, and tip points, parented to the wrist joint, then sweeping them into tapered rounded tubes colored like the glove material. Now I'm working out where the lantern attaches on the left hand.

I'm positioning the lantern to hang from the hand's grip point, checking its height against the floor, and parenting it to the wrist joint pointing downward -- then I'm planning a palm ring with a short chain of links connecting down to the lantern's bail for a more natural hanging look.

For the lantern itself I'm designing a hexagonal iron-and-glass build: a base plate, corner posts, glowing amber glass panes with an inner flame cone, a lathed hex roof cap, a finial ring, and an arc-swept bail handle, with the glass rendered as a low-poly glowing cylinder overlaid with iron lattice bars.

I'm texturing the glass panes with an SVG showing six side-by-side panes with mullions and a flame silhouette, keeping the glass opaque and glowing rather than transparent. Next I'm thinking through the belt at the coat's waist, planning to loft or sweep a loop around the hips using a torus or surface sweep.

Writing belt geometry logic...

For pouches I'll stick box geometry onto torso surface hits facing outward, and route a draped bandolier strap diagonally across the chest as a closed catmull loop. Along the front portion of that strap I'll place small glowing green vials with corks, oriented using frames that face along the strap's tangent.

For the satchel, I'm positioning a flap-and-buckle box at the right hip manually, roughly at the skirt region with the hips bone. Then I'm building the coat tail skirt as a lathe shell tapering from the waist radius down to a wider hem near the knee.

At the bottom the wall thickness is thin, around 0.02, and it tapers to about 0.15–0.17 near the top at the waist, so I'll keep smoothing at 0 for a low-poly faceted look with 14 segments. For paint, I'm thinking a coat texture with a tattered, mud-darkened hem and a visible front seam line. I also need to check that the legs don't poke through the skirt — comparing leg radius against the skirt's inner radius at that height to make sure there's clearance.

For the legs in rest pose, I'm keeping them slightly apart in an A-pose, with hip and ankle offsets. For the hem tatters, I'm placing a ring of hanging card fragments around the hem, reorienting each frame to face upward rather than outward so they hang naturally downward, attached to a hips bone with some randomized variation via the card generator. The bottom of these hanging tatters should sit above the boots, so I need to size them so they don't clip into the footwear.

Now for the hat, I'm constructing it as a single lathe outline combining brim and crown into one solid shape, defining the profile points so the brim flares out then the crown tapers upward. I'm tilting the lathe axis slightly forward so the hat sits naturally on the head rather than perfectly vertical.

Next I'm adding a crimson band as a thin ring lathe at the crown base, a brass box buckle at the front, and a tucked black feather angled back along the side of the band.

For the mask, I'm painting stitch marks along the beak seam using angle-based masks for a top seam line and crossing dashes, plus a darkened gradient toward the tip. For the lenses, I'm using a torus for the brass rim facing forward and preparing the glass material next.

Still shaping beak curves...

Lower beak tip tucks under the upper tip, which reads correctly as a bird beak shape. For decorative rings around the beak, I'm working out how to position a small loop sweep using the path's tangent at a given point to orient the frame correctly.

For the nostril detail, I'm adding two tiny dark cylinders near the beak's root to suggest breather vents. I'm also sketching out dimensions for a hood sphere and inner mask sphere, positioning them slightly offset in depth to create the falconry hood look.

I'm checking the geometry so the mask stays mostly recessed inside the hood, with the eye lenses poking out just barely at the front — the math confirms they clear the hood surface by a small margin, which should look right once I add the rim torus around the opening.

Checking the geometry at that ring position, the mask pokes slightly past the hood's cross-section there, but the rim torus conveniently covers that seam, so it still reads as a cowl framing the face. Now I'm extending that cowl into a draped cone shape down toward the shoulders.

For the capelet, I'm planning a lathe shell over the chest from narrow at the neck to wider at y=1.24, but I realize a circular cone that wide at the front would stick out unrealistically far given how shallow the torso actually is, so I need to adjust the bandolier and vial placement to sit lower, below the capelet's hem.

Since scale isn't directly supported, I'll use raw LatheGeometry for the capelet and skirt so I can squash the z-axis into an elliptical shape, then work out the painting coordinates using model-space position and normal rather than lathe UVs, defining the front slit by checking where x is near zero and z is positive.

Checking for collisions, I'm computing where the arm geometry would intersect the capelet's surface by interpolating the capelet's radius at the shoulder height and comparing it to the arm's x-position at that same y, confirming the arm pokes through the capelet near that point so the sleeve tube needs adjusting.

I'm thinking through the torso proportions and deciding the shoulders can stay simple since the capelet covers that area, and that the neck can be a short hidden tube. For the coat, I'm settling on a dark charcoal-brown palette with warm highlights, cooler shadows toward the bottom, and muddy tones at the hem, following a Darkest Dungeon-inspired color scheme with named hex values for coat, crimson, leather, bone, and brass tones.

I'm considering how to fake the thick black ink outlines and crosshatched shading typical of that gothic woodcut style — using normal-based ring detection for outlines and a diagonal hatching function that darkens pixels in shadowed areas, though I'm wary that 1cm hatch spacing might be too fine given the texture resolution.

I'm settling on a bumped-up paint resolution of 2048 with hatch lines spaced 2cm apart at 35% width, and sketching out a "DD shading" function that blends a lightened warm tone in lit areas, plain base color in midtones, and darker ink hatching in shadow based on the dot product between the surface normal and a light direction, plus some grime noise layered on top.

For the legs, I'm figuring trousers stay mostly hidden under the coat hem and boots, tapering the radius from thigh to ankle, then adding a leather boot shaft that sweeps along the lower leg chain from just above the knee joint down to the ankle, using the chain's joint parameters to crop the sweep range correctly.

I realize the full leg chain extends ankle to toe as a separate span, which would bend sharply at the ankle if swept continuously, so I'm cropping the trouser sweep to stop at the ankle and treating the foot/boot as its own geometry attached at the ankle joint, with a small ring or lathe shape forming the boot cuff at the top.

Now I'm adding details like a capsule-shaped knee brace, a thin strap ring with a brass buckle box on the shin, and lofting the boot foot shape from heel to toe stations.

Setting up the leg joint chain with hip, knee, ankle, and toe positions, then defining trouser and boot shaft radii that taper across the leg's length.

For accessories, I'll leave the right hand empty but add belt charms like a bird skull, bandolier vials, and a hanging herb bundle for character. Now I'm working out the lantern's position by computing the grip point relative to the wrist and palm geometry so it hangs naturally from the hand.

Still computing lantern dimensions...

I'm checking clearance — the lantern sits well clear of the skirt's outer radius, confirmed by the arm length. For the lantern hinge joint, I'll parent it to wristL with a downward hanging direction so animators can swing it, and I'm skipping the hinge role since that's reserved for lids/flaps. Now I'm building the lantern's parts: a torus loop as the hand strap around the palm, followed by a short chain of small tori links hanging down.

Adding chain and bail geometry...

Adding the base lathe shape, drip finial, roof vents, and warm amber flame glow inside the glass panes. I'm also planning rivets around the lens rims using a ring of small spheres, and starting on bandolier vials glowing green.

Then I'm fleshing out the belt details—a big brass buckle, bird-skull pendant, three pouches—plus coat buttons and stitch decals, tallying up roughly 200+ parts across body, fingers, rivets, vials, lantern, hat, and tatters.

Now I'm planning the key textures: a glowing amber-green lens eye with reflection highlight, glass lantern panes, tattered grey cloth strips with holes, a small parchment vial label with a skull, and an embroidered alchemical sigil on the satchel flap. I'm also considering a buckle texture and a hanging herb sprig card.

I'm settling on six textures total — LENS, GLASS, TATTER, SIGIL, LABEL, and HERB — while noting that textured parts should only render on front faces using plane geometry.

Now I'm working out the paint system: lighting direction, glow handling for textured surfaces, and a shading helper that mixes a base color toward ink for shadows and toward a warm highlight tone for lit areas.

Writing paint helper functions...

Finishing the hatch logic for underside faces, then confirming resolve is exported from paint.ts so the mix function works correctly with string or Rgb color inputs. The hatching applies diagonally in model space, which works fine since paint is baked per part in rest pose.

Now I'm detailing the coat paint, adding weathered grain texture with grime and mud staining near the hem and front slit seam. For the mask I'm layering a mottled pattern with hatching and visible stitch lines, and for the beak I'm setting up seam and stitch placement using clock-position coordinates, though I need to nail down whether that angular coordinate runs 0 to 360 or -180 to 180.

I'm now defining the skeleton hierarchy, starting with the hips as root and building the spine/chest chain, but I'm noticing the first spine joint sits at nearly the same position as the hips joint, which could create a zero-length bone I'll need to account for.

Continuing outward, I'm placing the neck, head, and jaw joints with appropriate aim directions, then setting up the torso loft between hip and chest stations. For limbs, I'm attaching the arm chains to the chest and the leg chains to the hips, tagging each with their role (arm, leg, digit), and adding a lantern joint parented to the left wrist for the finger/accessory detail.

I'm skipping extra hat and coat-tail joints since they aren't essential to the rig, keeping the skirt rigid on the hips instead. Now I'm double-checking the API surface -- joint creation with parent/at/aim/dir/role params, chain creation from point arrays producing one joint per span, sweep taking a radius array keyed over the swept range, and loft taking stations with an associated bone list and color.

Beyond those, I'm noting the rest of the available primitives: lathe for revolved outlines, part for placing geometry with transforms and texture, stick for embedding geometry with hit regions, surface helpers like ray/around/loop/drape/nearest for projecting onto a target, cards for billboard-style frame arrangements, extrude for outline-based shapes with bevel and smoothing, ring for repeating geometry along a line, and rod/capsule/spike for simple primitive shapes, plus a frame helper for getting position and direction from a spline.

I also need a glow helper imported from the kits path, and since hit ray results might return null, I should write a small `must` helper that throws with a label when a lookup fails instead of silently continuing. I'm also checking details like `along` for distributing callbacks across a path with from/to bounds, chain point lookups via `.at(t)`, sweep options on chain sources, builder creation with paint size and metadata export, and a rivet helper for marking attachment points.

Now I'm sketching out the SVG textures: the lens texture uses a radial gradient circle with sickly yellow-green tones fading to dark edges plus a white reflection crescent, while the glass texture divides into six panes with amber gradients, flame shapes, and dark iron mullions between them.

I'm checking that the six glass panes align with the cylinder's six radial segments so pane boundaries land exactly on the geometry's vertex corners, then starting on the tattered cloth texture with a jagged grey strip for the bottom edge.

For the tatter shape, I'm drawing the root edge fixed at the bottom attachment point and letting the ragged torn end hang free at the top, rendered in tinted grey tones so the card's color string can recolor it. Now moving to the sigil emblem, sketching a stitched leather background with a red alchemical cross design.

Setting up remaining decal designs: a parchment skull label marked "XII", a dried olive-brown herb sprig tucked into the hatband, and a dark iridescent raven feather, before moving into writing the actual module code.

Writing module imports and setup...

Building the arm chains...

Still shaping the cuff and glove geometry...

For the glove box, I'm using the wrist frame for orientation with position set separately, sizing it thin in X, longer in Y along the arm, and wider in Z. I'll color the gloves dark leather, then start planning four fingers positioned off the knuckle base with varying forward offsets and lengths.

Writing finger placement code...

Still computing torus geometry...

Still working out lantern geometry...

Still defining lantern geometry...

I'm adding the drip cone at the base, checking total height stays under budget, and working out the rotational alignment between the hexagonal glass cylinder and posts so the facets and corners line up correctly using lathe/cylinder angle conventions.

Writing material definitions for iron and brass with tarnish and verdigris, then setting up the lathe geometry for the lantern's hat shape.

Positioning the hat relative to the hood and skull — checking cross-sectional radii so the hat crown sits visibly above the hood without clipping through it, and giving it a slight backward tilt for the plague doctor look.

I'm shaping the hat's lathe profile with a wide brim, curved crown, and dark mottled felt paint, then adding a crimson band around the base of the crown.

I'll simplify by keeping the hat axis vertical for the buckle placement, positioning a brass frame box with a darker inner box poking through front and back, plus a tongue bar. Then I'm working out the feather geometry, extruding its outline and angling it up and back from the left side of the band.

I'm shaping the feather's outline with a smooth curve defining its quill length and width, then painting the rachis line in bone color with darker barb streaks and an iridescent tip, plus a smaller crimson companion feather. Then I'm placing herb sprigs on cards near the band and framing the mask's skull shape using a scaled sphere geometry.

Now I'm building the hood as another scaled sphere sitting over the head, checking that it overlaps cleanly with the capelet below, and adding a torus rim around the hood's edge for a finished bone-colored border.

Scaling the torus to match the mask's elliptical cross-section, I'm sizing it to roughly 0.108 by 0.119 with a 0.022 tube, then double-checking it doesn't poke into the eye lenses positioned at ±0.05 along x.

Now I'm calculating the eye lens placement by casting a ray against the mask surface to find the hit point and normal, then positioning a small torus rim there oriented along that normal.

The glass lens disc sits recessed slightly behind the rim as a flat tangent circle, but since the mask sphere curves away from that tangent plane, I need to check whether the sphere surface pokes through near the disc's edges.

For rivets around the lens, placing them on a flat ring would leave them floating above the curved surface since the sphere dips inward with distance from center. Instead I should project each rivet position onto the mask surface directly, finding the nearest point on the sphere for each ring item before placing the sphere geometry.

Now I'm sketching the beak as a bezier curve defined by four control points, with a radius function that tapers from wide at the base to a point at the tip, using round and point caps respectively, and checking the beak's top position relative to the eye placement.

Still working out the overlap issue: the beak root is cutting into the lens region, so I'm adjusting the lens y-position and beak root dimensions until their bottom edges clear each other cleanly.

Checking the mask sphere's surface depth at the beak root confirms it sits buried inside, giving a clean round-cap transition. Now I'm defining the upper beak and jaw curves as control point sequences with tapering radii along their length.

Jaw tip sits lower and further back, which looks right. I'm setting up the jaw joint with the head as parent, aiming toward the jaw tip. For the beak's brass band, I'm placing a frame along the upper beak path and sweeping a thin brass ring around it, double-checking that the loop sits outside the mask area rather than buried inside it.

Now I'm adding nostril vents as small dark cylinders embedded on either side of the upper beak top, plus brass ring details underneath using additional cylinder sticks. The beak stitching will be handled through paint rather than geometry.

For the leather strap circling the head above the mask, I'm working out how to drape a band loop across the hood at eye level using a world-up direction reference.

Setting the strap at y 1.70 so it wraps the hood horizontally -- it'll stay hidden where it crosses the mask front but show on the sides and back, so I'm adding a buckle detail there instead of rivets. Now I'm starting the torso loft stations, defining width and height at increasing heights along the body.

Still defining loft stations and bone rigging...

For the neck I'm adding a short dark rod hidden under the hood, then switching to a lathed skirt geometry with a closed profile, scaling it slightly to flatten the silhouette and defining outer radius points going down from the hips.

Finishing the inner contour points of the skirt profile and closing the loop, I decide to use flat shading on the 16-segment lathe so the facets give that painterly low-poly look, then move to texturing the skirt surface based on its UVs.

Checking proportions, the skirt radius at the waist ends up slightly larger than the torso there, which actually works since the belt will sit at y=1.0 and cover the seam—except I realize the torso radius at that height is smaller than the skirt's, so the belt would get hidden underneath the skirt geometry instead of sitting visibly on top. I'm reconsidering how to define the belt loop so it wraps around the correct silhouette, maybe by taking the smallest surface loop at that cutting plane across both torso and skirt.

Maybe simpler to construct the belt directly as a closed ellipse loop at a fixed radius and height rather than deriving it from the torso surface, so the dimensions are exact. I'll try a surface loop cut on the torso at y=1.0 with a small lift, though I'm wary the loft's cap might interfere with how the cutting plane intersects the body.

Now I'm positioning a brass belt buckle via a ray cast against the torso surface, then placing pouches around the belt at a few angles with leather box shapes, flap details, and brass studs. I'm also planning a satchel at the hip with explicit box geometry dimensions and rotation to hang naturally below the belt.

I'm positioning the satchel flap and sigil decal, then figuring out a strap that drapes diagonally from the hip up to the opposite shoulder using a closed catmull-rom curve.

For the crossing bandolier strap, I'm plotting another diagonal to form an X across the chest, noting it stays mostly hidden under the capelet above a certain height but visible lower down. I'm now working out where to place vials along the bandolier's lower front, raycasting against the torso to find accurate attachment points.

Checking against the capelet's hem geometry, I realize it hangs about 8cm proud of the chest at the front, so vials placed too high would get hidden under it — I need to keep them in the lower range, just below the capelet's hem.

Checking the shoulder region more carefully — at various heights the capelet radius seems to just barely clear the torso and sleeve widths, with only a slight poke-out near the shoulder top that's probably negligible.

For the tattered hem effect, I'm working out positions around the capelet's elliptical rim using angle-based placement with the frames leaning outward and facing up, while making sure to skip any tatter cards where the arms would pierce through near the sides.

Checking the skirt's own tatter ring similarly, with its own hem radius and ellipse scaling, leaving a gap at the front for the slit. Now I'm positioning the coat's front buttons along the torso, figuring out their vertical placement under the capelet and whether they form one or two columns for a double-breasted look.

Skipping the back scroll idea, but adding a small bone-colored bird skull charm hanging from the belt's left front, plus an herb bundle with texture cards at the left hip. Lantern, lenses, and vials together serve as the character's light sources. Boots get a mud gradient near the ground mixing into the leather, trousers are a dark grey-brown, and hands get gloves with cuffs.

Now I'm setting up the skeleton structure: naming leg chain joints per side (hip, knee, ankle, toe), defining the spine-to-chest chain with its path points, then adding neck and head joints with specific positions and aim targets to establish the rig hierarchy.

I'm continuing with jaw, hood/mask, and capelet bone assignments to head and chest, then setting up torso loft bones and ensuring arm chains parent correctly from chest with shoulder/elbow/wrist naming, finishing with a lantern joint attached to the wrist.

Writing SVG lens texture...

Still writing flame and lattice shapes...

I confirm the card's root sits at the bottom, matching the drawing's bottom edge, with the ragged torn edge at the top from the hanging lean. I'm also planning a darker seam band near the root for shading, then sketching a colored sigil icon with a dashed border and a crosshair motif inside a circle.

I'm thinking through an alchemical symbol design combining circle, triangle, and cross shapes, plus a small parchment-style label with a tiny skull icon and text. For the herb icon I'm picturing an olive stem with rotated leaf ellipses and a red twine tying the root at the bottom, and considering whether a feather texture card fits the hat-band herb layout too.

Now I'm deciding texture placement on the band—feather on the left, herbs on the right—and considering extra mask details like a small dried-blood spatter decal near the beak tip for a grittier feel. I'm counting up six core textures (lens, glass, tatter, sigil, label, herb) and weighing whether to add a seventh, like a wax seal or tucked scroll, but leaning toward skipping it to keep things simple.

Settling on six textures as sufficient, I'm moving into defining the paint function, setting up lighting direction and ink/warm/cool color constants, then writing a shader-like function that blends base color with warm and cool tones based on light angle and adds grime.

Still writing paint logic...

Deciding against that edge darkening since it breaks side views. Now I'm setting up the coat wool texture with a grain pattern and building the skirt paint function with an ink front seam and mud resolution logic layered on the coat base.

I'm adding a crimson trim band near the hem with a zigzag pattern for the plague doctor coat, then moving on to mottled base tones for the mask material.

For stitching details, I'm defining a vertical center-front seam that renders as alternating dashes of ink and leather based on position, and for the beak I'm adding dark stitching along the top and sides, crossing stitches near the tip, and a gradual darkening toward the point.

Now I'm setting up the material palettes for the hood, hat, leather, crimson cloth, and gloves using mottled grain textures with grime and hatching overlays.

I'm defining the boot and trouser paints, plus brass and iron metal finishes with tarnish and verdigris, and a flat bone color, then noting the flat glow colors for vials and glass textures.

I'm figuring out a dark nostril tint, tattered color strings for the coat and capelet, and checking SDK signatures for loft stations, cards, frame orientation, and the hand palm part attached to the wrist bone.

Now I'm designing the fingers as sweep chains with tapered radii and rounded fingertip caps, positioning the knuckle bases inside the palm and the thumb base slightly forward, then spacing the four fingers along the palm width with a slight fan angle so they don't overlap too much.

For the torso, I'm computing a surface from the loft geometry so straps like the bandolier and satchel can drape onto it — using a closed catmull-rom path that gets pulled onto the torso surface and then swept into a leather strap, checking that the loop crosses the left shoulder properly without clipping into other geometry.

I'm deciding strap cross-sections should probably use a simple round sweep rather than a box, since orientation of a flat section along the path is uncertain; a small-radius circle keeps things safe. For the belt I'll sweep a closed loop around the torso at the waist height, and now I'm figuring out where pouches should attach relative to that belt line.

Since the skirt bulges out past the torso near the waist, I realize pouches should be positioned by casting rays against the skirt's surface rather than the torso, firing a horizontal ray outward from the skirt's center at that height to find the true outer hit point.

Setting the pouch box dimensions so its thickness runs along the surface normal and its height follows the flow direction up the body, then adding a smaller flap box stuck to the same hit point but shifted upward slightly.

Now I'm placing the studs on the pouch front, then working out the skirt and torso button placements using ray casts against the surface geometry, and planning a small bird-skull charm hanging from a cord off the belt's front-left.

I'm hanging the herb bundle upside down from the twine at the root, mimicking real dried herbs, and skipping extra hat decoration in favor of feathers. For the capelet, I'm adding a brass chain clasp with two round discs placed symmetrically at the front top, working out their position based on the torso and capelet curvature at that height.

Now I'm positioning the clasp discs slightly lower, checking that the chain sags naturally between them and that the beak's jaw hangs just above it without overlapping, then starting to figure out where the hood's bottom edge meets the collar.

Deciding to skip extra details like a glowing lantern flame, skull motif, rosary, or pauldrons to keep the design focused. I'm now defining the tatter cards for the hem using a flow function that assigns each card a direction and slight random variation in size and color, then moving on to figure out the skirt's circumference for sizing the hem pieces.

Now I'm sizing the hem cards based on the skirt's circumference and working out the leg geometry, including contact points and bone roles for the spine, head, and neck. I'm setting up the feet with a rigid loft bone for the ankle joint and boxes for the sole and heel block, defining their dimensions and attachment positions.

Checking foot clearances — making sure the heel block, sole, and toe cap radius all fit without overlapping the ground or sticking out past each other. Now I'm adding boot buckle straps as rods along the leg, sized slightly wider than the boot itself, with a brass buckle attached to the strap's surface.

Simplifying the buckle placement to a box positioned just above the knee joint. Then I'm computing leg segment lengths (hip-knee, knee-ankle, ankle-toe) to get normalized t-values for the chain, which I'll use to sweep the trouser leg with tapering radii up to the knee point, capping the end round.

Now adding the boot shaft and fold-down cuff sweeps along the leg chain with flat/round caps, then checking whether the skirt (which is a closed lathe shape down to the hem) actually hides the knee and boot cuff from view.

Since the skirt hides most of the boot above the hem, I'll keep boots visible only from 0 to 0.30 and move the buckle straps lower to y=0.2 and 0.12, dropping the now-hidden cuff detail to save on geometry.
